item.title: Filling In the Blanks in Dementia
item.description:
Dementia

Filling In the Blanks in Dementia

Comprehending the yardsticks for good caregiving.

Posted August 24, 2026

You can’t remember what you don’t remember…

There are days when I don’t remember much, so I write everything down. It offers some peace for those, like me, with Alzheimer’s and other dementias.

I suppose in some ways misery loves company. And I have a lot of company in this journey. More than 55 million people worldwide live with dementia—a number, experts say, that’s expected to nearly double in 20 years, reaching an estimated 139 million by 2050.

And the impacts on caregivers is astounding in terms of health and personal costs. Caregivers themselves are often plagued with high anxiety and great depression. And unpaid caregivers provide the equivalent of nearly $470 billion a year in free care.

I’m trying to make more sense of all this. So, I recently sat in my studio on Outer Cape Cod with an expert—Suzanne Faith, a psychiatric nurse and a Certified Dementia Professional (CDP) for 40 years. She’s a caregiving expert, former director of the Alzheimer’s caregiver support program at Cape Cod Healthcare, author of the newly released Dementia Engagement: A Definitive Guide to Alzheimer’s and Dementia Activities, and a good friend.

She counseled me in an interview on the fundamentals of dementia caregiving and how to engage those suffering from the disease.

I’ve dealt with both. Years ago, I was a family caregiver for my parents, both of whom passed away from the disease, which also took my maternal grandfather and paternal uncle. I’ve been blessed, doctors tell me, with resilient cognitive reserve and “neuroplasticity”—the brain’s natural ability at times to reconnect brain paths in synapses, thus allowing a neuron, almost robotically, to pass an electrical or chemical signal to another cell despite disease.

(Had to look that up; I barely passed basic biology in high school.)

Why Understanding Brain Changes Is Critical for Caregiving

The success of caregiving, Faith tells me, depends on understanding the changes that are occurring in the brain and learning how to communicate differently:

“In the early stages of Alzheimer’s, language becomes compromised; both the ability to find the right words as well as comprehend what is being said. Caregivers need to understand this. Comprehending words and teasing out their meaning requires abstract understanding, which a person with dementia can no longer do, especially with the fast pace we often speak. Instead, caregivers should speak slowly and use simple language.”

In caregiving, Faith says, “Knowing how the disease progresses can help caregivers adjust their strategies for care. For example, there are four lobes of the brain, each commanding their own unique set of functions. In Alzheimer’s disease, the first lobes to be compromised are the temporal and frontal lobes. If caregivers understand that the frontal lobe controls planning and initiating ideas and the temporal lobe controls language and hearing, compensating for these losses and adjusting how one communicates will lead to greater successes throughout the day.”

Many caregivers, Faith notes, often mistakenly think that those in their care do not want to do anything, and instead seem to prefer just sitting and watching television or staring out the window. “What is happening in their brain is that those with dementia simply don’t understand what a caregiver is asking, which requires them to visualize the concept and follow through with a choice. Since we’re all hardwired to respond to pleas for help, asking someone with dementia for help in performing a task often yields a greater degree of successful engagement.”

Another strategy for caregivers is combining verbal and nonverbal cues at the same time: “For example,” she adds, “offering a choice of two meals or clothing options and having them point to their preference. This avoids the use of relying on words to indicate what they want and preserves their dignity.”

Instinct, Routine, and Safety in Dementia Care

For strategy purposes, Faith often asks caregivers to imagine they are visiting a foreign country and don’t speak the language: thus, how would one communicate needs? It’s a difficult process for both the patient and a family caregiver. “With dementia, you have two victims—the person with the disease and the caregiver,” she explains. “It can be incredibly difficult for both, as the individual with dementia requires more care and the family member is grieving over the loss of a person that they knew. We should be compassionate to both and their respective plights.”

Faith says that in this decline, “it is essential to preserve the dignity of the one suffering from dementia. Having a disability doesn’t mean that you are less of a person. When shown personal dignity, those with dementia know instinctively that there’s an emotional connection even though they may not recognize the person.”

Instinct, she adds, often is not robbed in early stages of dementia, so it’s important to stick to a routine: “Those with dementia need to feel safe and secure. Without memory to ground them to their world, they are free-floating through the day. This is where a daily routine is important. No surprises. Routine helps those with dementia feel safe, which is a constant concern. It’s a horrifying cycle.”

So those with dementia, Faith says, often adopt the mantra of “I want to go home...I want to go home!... What they actually are expressing by this phrase is: ‘I want to feel safe.’”

I relate to this in my own journey. Years ago when I could still drive, I was heading “home” to Cape Cod after a late-night meeting in Boston. I kept thinking of my childhood and wanted to reconnect with it. At midnight, I was many miles away from Cape Cod on I-95 outside New Haven, driving “home” to Rye, New York in Westchester County, where I grew up just outside Manhattan.

My instincts, not my brain, told me to “go home.” I wanted to feel safe...It wasn’t until I was running out of gas that I realized where I was, turned around, and drove back home to Cape Cod, arriving about 3 am. The experience so frightened me…Still does.

And then there’s the common over-the-top rage in dementia when lights in the brain dim—akin to someone flicking lights off after dark. These are periods of overwhelming confusion and anxiety—again, a time for caregiver calm.

In her book, Dementia Engagement, written for both families and professional caregivers, Faith reinforces: “Celebrate every win, big or small. And remember, you’re not just doing activities; you’re building bridges, honoring stories, and making it through each day one success at a time.”

item.title: When Sex Happens During Sleep: How Sexsomnia Affects Couples
item.description:
Sex

When Sex Happens During Sleep: How Sexsomnia Affects Couples

Sexual behaviors during sleep, termed "sexsomnia," can impact both the sleeper and their partner.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Sexsomnia involves unintentional sexual behaviors while asleep.
  • Sexsomnia behaviors can impact couples in complex ways, and may lead to feelings of insecurity and mistrust.
  • Even though sexsomnic behaviors are not intentional, they do impact one's partners.
  • Couples dealing with sexsomnia need to discuss shared plans to manage the impact of the behaviors.

Sexsomnia is a disorder where a person engages in sexual behavior while asleep. They may masturbate, make sexual sounds, touch a partner, or initiate intercourse. Because the person isn't fully awake, they often remember little or nothing the next morning.

One thing that is clear is that it impacts couples as much or even more than it may impact the individual with sexsomnia. The gap in conscious awareness of sexual behaviors is especially difficult for couples. The behavior happens to both partners, but only one remembers it.

“How Can You Not Remember?” Making Sense of the Sexsomnia Memory Gap

The experience of unequal memories can create confusion and mistrust in couples. In one case, a man regularly initiated sex with his wife during sleep almost every night—but had no memory of it. When he later complained that they weren't having enough sex, his wife reminded him of their nighttime encounters. He assumed she was making excuses and lying, rather than having sex with him.

In another case, a woman made sexual sounds, rubbed against pillows and appeared to orgasm while asleep. When her husband finally told her, she initially thought he was making it up. Even after he awakened her during or immediately after episodes, she still couldn't remember what had happened.

Source: © Vyacheslav Argenberg/Wikimedia Commons; CC BY 4.0

For the observing partner, the events are real and memorable. For the person with sexsomnia, they may feel impossible to believe. Without an explanation, both partners may begin questioning each other’s honesty or perceptions.

Sexsomnia Can Trigger Insecurity and Jealousy

Sleep-related sexual behavior can look purposeful, even though it's occurring while unconscious. This can lead partners to interpret it as evidence of hidden wishes or dissatisfaction.

In reality, sexual behaviors during sleep may not be related to a person's waking sexual interests. One man actually masturbated during sleep with a different hand than he used when awake, and one wife preferred making love to her sleeping husband because he engaged in more "primal" and unrestrained sex than when he was awake.

One husband whose wife talked during sleep sometimes heard her say the names of other people—never his own. Early in their marriage, he worried that he was not sexually satisfying her or that she secretly wanted someone else. Because he already carried sexual shame and insecurity, her nighttime behavior became “fuel” for criticizing himself, interfering in their sexual relationship.

But words or behaviors during a parasomnia shouldn't be treated as reliable confessions. A sleeping brain can produce sounds, names and actions without expressing a conscious preference or intention.

How Sexsomnia-Driven Shame Can Silence Both Partners

The person with sexsomnia may feel embarrassed, guilty or frightened after learning what they have done. One woman apologized when told that she had spoken the names of people the couple knew or had referred to women. Her husband eventually became selective about what he reported because he did not want to intensify her shame over her nighttime behaviors.

Partners may also remain silent. They may fear embarrassing the person, starting an argument or being disbelieved. In one case, the behavior continued for 13 years before it was discussed openly in a sleep clinic. This is a common pattern - most people experience sexsomnia for years before seeking treatment.

Silence is understandable, but it can allow confusion and resentment to grow. It may also delay recognition of an underlying sleep problem.

The Complexities of Consent and Safety in Cases of Sexsomnia

Sexsomnia is not intentional misconduct—the sleeping person is not consciously choosing the behavior. At the same time, lack of intent does not erase their partner’s experience.

A partner may feel startled, pressured, unsafe or violated, particularly when the behavior was not previously discussed. Unintended pregnancies can even result from sexsomnia behaviors. In some, sexsomnia episodes caused significant distress and deterioration of the relationship; even ultimate divorce.

Couples dealing with sexsomnia need an explicit nighttime safety plan, including plans for contraception when one partner is not fully conscious. This might include sleeping separately, using separate bedding or rooms, reducing access to triggering situations and agreeing that sexual contact should stop unless both people are clearly awake and able to communicate consent.

Sexsomnia Can Disrupt a Couple's Sexual Relationship

Nighttime behavior may affect daytime intimacy. In one case, the wife sometimes declined sex because the couple had already been sexually active during the night—something her husband could not remember. To him, her refusal felt like rejection. To her, his request ignored an encounter she had already experienced.

Sexsomnia can therefore create mismatched perceptions of sexual frequency, satisfaction, and initiation. Couples may argue about a sexual relationship that they are, quite literally, experiencing differently.

Understanding of Sexsomnia Could Bring Couples Closer Together

Not every effect is negative. The couple who discussed the wife’s sexual vocalizations eventually used those conversations to talk more openly about fantasies, sexual attraction, and sexual shame. Through her sexsomnia, she came to accept and admit that she was bisexual. Her husband came to see the episodes less as evidence that he was inadequate and more as one part of her complex sexual self.

This does not mean couples should romanticize sexsomnia. It means that accurate information, compassion and honest communication can replace some of the fear and secrecy surrounding it. Discussing these issues and feelings in therapy can help couples' to process the experience in a healthy way.

Source: Image by Pexels from Pixabay

Sexsomnia is Treatable, But It Needs Proper Evaluation

Episodes may become more frequent with stress, sleep deprivation, or irregular schedules. In one case, work pressure and insomnia worsened the behavior. In another, treating sleep apnea stopped the episodes.

Evaluation by a qualified clinician is important. Treatment depends on the individual and may involve improving sleep habits, addressing stress, treating another sleep disorder, therapy or medication.

Most importantly, couples should approach sexsomnia as a shared problem requiring both accountability for its impact and compassion for unconscious behaviors. Naming the condition does not solve every relational injury—but it can give couples a more accurate and less blaming place to begin.

item.title: Good News for Anyone Who’s Ever Felt Awkward
item.description:
Anxiety

Good News for Anyone Who’s Ever Felt Awkward

Those who cringe most are often the ones who care most.

Posted August 24, 2026

Source: Smooth Models/Pexels

You wave back at someone who was waving at the person behind you. You call your teacher "Mom." You watch a contestant sing wildly off-key on live television and cringe. Awkwardness is one of the most universal human experiences and one of the most quietly painful. Yet for something so ordinary, it turns out to be psychologically rich. Decades of research reveal that awkwardness isn't a personal flaw or a sign of social incompetence. It's a window into how deeply we are wired to care about belonging.

It's not that you lack social skills

In a landmark study, psychologist Rowland Miller found that people who are easily embarrassed are not less socially skilled than everyone else. What sets them apart is how intensely they care whether their behavior is appropriate, and how motivated they are to avoid disapproval.

Miller found that shyness and embarrassability are different things. Shyness is tied to low social confidence, a sense of not being good at interacting. Embarrassability is about caring, perhaps too much, about doing the right thing in front of others. You can be socially skilled and still cringe constantly, precisely because you are attuned to every unwritten rule in the room.

In other words, awkwardness is often a byproduct of caring. The people who feel it most acutely are frequently those most invested in being decent, considerate, and socially "correct."

Why a small slip can feel catastrophic

If awkwardness is about caring, then the depth of the pain comes from what we believe is at stake. Researchers David Moscovitch and colleagues studied how people appraise social "blunders"—a trip on the stairs, a mispronounced name, a joke followed by silence. They found that more socially anxious people systematically overestimate the consequences of these moments. They expect harsher judgment, longer memories, and more relational fallout than actually occur.

This overestimation held even when participants imagined someone else committing the blunder. The problem wasn't a distorted sense of themselves specifically. It was a belief that social standards are extremely high and rigid, that there is a strict code, and that breaking it carries real punishment. When you hold that belief, a minor slip doesn't feel minor. It feels like evidence you've failed a test everyone else is passing.

The "second-hand cringe" is real because it's in your brain

Some of the most fascinating research explains why we squirm watching someone else's embarrassing moment, even a stranger or a fictional character. This vicarious awkwardness, the cringe you feel during a painful scene in a sitcom, reflects empathy in action.

Source: Pavel Danilyuk/Pexels

Neuroscientists led by Shisei Tei scanned people's brains while they watched others perform badly and react with either genuine embarrassment or oblivious pride. They identified two different empathy systems at work. One is affective empathy: the automatic sharing of another person's emotion, involving brain regions like the amygdala and insula. The other is cognitive empathy: the more deliberate act of taking someone's perspective, involving regions associated with reflective thinking.

For most of us, these systems work together. But the researchers found that in people whose social anxiety is dominated by fear of embarrassing others, the balance tips toward raw emotional contagion over reflective perspective-taking. That imbalance can make embarrassing situations harder to process and more overwhelming. The cringe in these cases, it seems, is empathy running slightly hot.

Untangling shyness, awkwardness, and anxiety

Everyday language blurs these words together, and so, to some extent, does the science. When researchers Christina Brook and Teena Willoughby examined ten different questionnaires measuring shyness and social anxiety, they found that both were dominated by the same underlying theme: fear of negative evaluation, self-consciousness, and the dread of being scrutinized.

What did stand out as genuinely separate was sociability, the simple desire to be around others. You can crave connection and still fear judgment. That combination, wanting closeness while bracing for rejection, may be the emotional engine behind much of what we call awkwardness.

When awkwardness becomes something more

For most people, awkwardness is a passing sting. But for some, the fear of humiliation becomes organizing and life-limiting. At the clinical extreme, avoidant personality disorder is defined by pervasive social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, and hypersensitivity to criticism—including avoiding new activities specifically because they might prove embarrassing.

There's also emerging evidence that embarrassing experiences can leave lasting marks. Research suggests that accidental, non-hostile embarrassing events can provoke reactions resembling those caused by bullying, and that these reactions can feed later social anxiety. Awkward moments, in other words, are not always trivial.

Making peace with the cringe

The research offers a reframe. Awkwardness is not proof that you're bad at being with people. It's usually proof that you care about them. This includes caring about perceived social rules, others' moods, and others' comfort.

Perhaps if awkwardness is fueled by the belief that social standards are rigid and the consequences severe, then the antidote is gently testing that belief. Most blunders are forgotten within minutes. Most people are far more preoccupied with their own missteps than with yours. And the flush of embarrassment itself, research suggests, actually signals to others that you're trustworthy and care about the relationship.

Source: Andrea Piacquadio/Pexels

The next time you wave at the wrong person, it may help to remember: the cringe is not a defect. It's your social conscience doing its job. While you're at it, maybe just keep on waving. Own it. Feel it. Awkward. The good news is that you've survived. The bad news is that your brain may bring it up again in 2034.
